summary: This informational memo defines the common architecture for Multicast Security key management. It introduces the group security association, a shared set of security settings for a group, and describes the protocols that establish it. The architecture supports security protocols at various layers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4046 describes how a group controller can admit members and give them the keys needed for secure group communication. It separates initial registration from later key updates and leaves the specific protocols to other documents.

subtitle: A common architecture for admitting members and distributing keys to secure groups.

tldr.problem: Group communication needs members to hold current keys as membership changes, but pairwise key exchange alone does not describe scalable group registration and rekeying.
tldr.mechanism: A Group Controller and Key Server authenticates members during registration and provides a group security association. An optional rekey protocol distributes later key updates.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4046 defines an Informational architecture, not a wire protocol. It separates registration, rekeying and data security so different applications can choose suitable protocols.

today: RFC 4046 is an Informational memo published in April 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document defines an architecture, not a wire protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The Multicast Security (MSEC) group key management architecture supports security protocols at the application, transport and network layers. It can serve one-to-many, many-to-many and one-to-one communication, with different key-management protocols selected for different applications.

The memo defines the Group Security Association (GSA) and describes registration and rekey protocols that can establish or update it. It provides common abstractions and design guidance, not a complete protocol format.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture provides a common way to organize group key management for different applications. It describes the functions and security associations, while other protocols define their messages.

sections.title: What Group Key Management Must Support
sections.content:
A group key-management protocol provides authorized members with current cryptographic state for secrecy and authentication. The memo lists 12 requirements, including secure delivery of keys, replay and denial-of-service protection, support for members joining and leaving, and recovery after key compromise.

A scalable rekey should not require a separate unicast exchange with every member. The architecture also aims to resist collusion by excluded members and to support the data-security protocol used by the application. The requirements are not exhaustive and do not apply to every group.
sections.plainLanguage: A group key protocol must keep keys private, update them as membership changes and help members recover after missed updates. It should do this without requiring a separate exchange with every member for each rekey.

sections.title: Registration and Rekeying
sections.content:
A group owner designates a Group Controller and Key Server (GCKS). During registration, the GCKS and a joining member mutually authenticate. If the member is authorized, the GCKS provides information to initialize the Data SA and, when the group uses rekey messages, the Rekey SA.

Later, the rekey protocol can update the Data SA or Rekey SA after membership or policy changes, key creation or key expiration. Rekey messages may be sent by multicast or unicast. The architecture separates registration from rekeying so applications can choose different ways to establish and update keys.
sections.plainLanguage: During registration, the GCKS checks a member and provides the security information it needs. Later rekey messages can update group keys without repeating the full registration exchange.

sections.title: The Three Associations in a GSA
sections.content:
A GSA combines three types of security association. The Registration SA is a unicast association between the GCKS and each member; it protects registration. The optional Rekey SA protects key-update messages and carries key-encryption and authentication information.

The Data SA contains the keys and policy used by the data-security protocol to protect group traffic. There may be separate Data SAs for different senders, one shared association for the group, or a combination. The Group identity and SPI together uniquely identify a Rekey SA; the SPI changes when the key-encryption keys change.
sections.plainLanguage: The GSA includes an association for registration, an optional one for key updates, and one or more for group data. The data association carries the keys and settings that the data-security protocol needs.

sections.title: Reliable Updates and Recovery
sections.content:
Rekey messages need confidentiality, authentication and replay protection. They can be encrypted with a group key-encryption key and authenticated with a message authentication code or a digital signature. The GCKS must ensure that members receive the current Data and Rekey SAs.

A member that misses a key update may contact the GCKS to register again, retrieve recent messages, or obtain posted updates. If many members request recovery at once, they can overwhelm the GCKS. The memo discusses random delays, feedback suppression and local repair servers as ways to reduce this implosion risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Rekey messages must be protected and delivered to members. A member that misses an update can resynchronize, but many simultaneous recovery requests may overload the key server.

sections.title: Security Limits and Status
sections.content:
Protocols based on this architecture must address man-in-the-middle, connection hijacking, replay, reflection and denial-of-service attacks. Shared group secrets create additional risks: a member may disclose them or impersonate a sender or the GCKS. Symmetric authentication of rekey messages is appropriate only when members can be trusted not to impersonate the GCKS or one another.

The memo says group policy is set externally rather than negotiated by this architecture. It identifies novelty and complexity as major risks and calls for further analysis of concrete protocol designs.
sections.plainLanguage: Every member who knows a shared key may expose it or misuse it. The architecture leaves policy and protocol details to other work and says concrete designs need careful analysis.
